summary: Suggests improvements to the NSFNET routing architecture to give clients of the backbone a more flexible interface. It is informational.

eli5.summary: The big network backbone needed better directions for the smaller networks attached to it. This proposes changes.

questions: why did nsfnet need egp instead of rip
how can one router handle both regional and backbone routing
subtitle: How to make the NSFNET backbone's interface simpler and cheaper for regional networks to connect.

tldr.problem: The NSFNET backbone requires regional networks to deploy and manage their own routing protocol peer, which is expensive and complex for smaller sites wanting to connect to the backbone.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes allowing two routing protocol instances (IGP and EGP/BGP) to run on a single router at the edge, communicating locally, so a regional network does not need to build and maintain separate hardware just for the backbone connection.
tldr.outcome: This architecture simplifies the interface for NSFNET clients while maintaining routing isolation and administrative control between the backbone and its attached networks.
tldr.outcomeLabel: A simpler path to the backbone

facts.label: Phase 2 backbone nodes
facts.value: 14, at supercomputer centers and mid-level network points

today: RFC 1222 is informational and was overtaken by developments in routing protocols and Internet infrastructure. BGP (Border Gateway Protocol, referenced in the RFC) became the standard exterior routing protocol for the Internet, and the single-router-with-two-daemons approach became common practice. The NSFNET backbone was later retired in 1995, replaced by distributed regional networks. However, the architectural principles described in the RFC—routing isolation, administrative separation, and the use of exterior protocols at network boundaries—remain fundamental to modern Internet routing design.

sections.title: What This RFC Proposes
sections.content:
RFC 1222 examines the evolution of NSFNET routing architecture and proposes a way to simplify the interface between the NSFNET backbone and its client networks. The authors, Hans-Werner Braun (San Diego Supercomputer Center) and Yakov Rekhter (IBM), draw lessons from the first two phases of NSFNET to make the third phase (running at 45 Mbps) more accessible to smaller research sites.

The core idea is architectural: maintain strict routing isolation between the backbone and client networks (a good design principle proven over time) but relax the implementation requirement that clients must buy separate equipment just to achieve this isolation.
sections.eli5: The NSFNET is the big highway connecting computer networks. This document says how to make it easier for smaller networks to hook up to the highway without buying extra equipment.

sections.title: Phase 1: The 56 Kbps Backbone
sections.content:
The original NSFNET Phase 1 backbone ran at 56 Kbps using Hello Protocol for routing. Regional networks connected via gatedaemon, which translated between Hello (on the backbone) and RIP (Routing Information Protocol, the standard in mid-level networks). While this worked, the architecture created problems: metric fluctuations and routing changes rippled across the entire system. Routing loops formed easily because there was no clear separation between the backbone routing and client routing.

The gatedaemon did allow site administrators to filter routes by IP network numbers, giving some control, but the overall system was unstable. Six nodes of Phase 1 were located at NSF-funded supercomputer centers.
sections.eli5: The first version was slow and unstable. If the routing rules changed at one end, the changes spread everywhere, sometimes causing confusion and loops.

sections.title: Phase 2: The T1 Backbone and Strong Decoupling
sections.content:
Phase 2 (1.5 Mbps T1 lines) learned from these problems and strongly decoupled the backbone's internal routing from client networks' routing. The interface between backbone and clients was built using EGP (Exterior Gateway Protocol), which signals only network reachability (up or down), not metric fluctuations. This provides two benefits: routing isolation and the ability to engineer the distribution of routing information.

Phase 2 introduced a centralized routing configuration database, with a computer system ensuring correctness before distributing configuration to all backbone nodes. This architecture is more stable and scalable. Fourteen nodes in Phase 2 were located at supercomputer centers and mid-level network attachment points.
sections.eli5: The second version separated the backbone routing from regional routing. The backbone and regions only exchanged simple 'yes, I have this route' or 'no, I do not' messages, not detailed metrics. This made the system much more stable.

sections.title: Phase 3: The T3 Backbone with a Simpler Interface
sections.content:
Phase 3 (45 Mbps, implemented by 1991) uses a new architecture in which core nodes are co-located with telephone company switching facilities, forming a two-dimensional cloud infrastructure. Individual sites connect via exterior nodes (E-NSS) with a single T3 access line to a core node (C-NSS). From the client perspective, the routing interface is identical to Phase 2: the same EGP/BGP protocol is used.

The paper authors propose that for Phase 3 and beyond, it should be possible for a single router at the client site to run two instances of routing daemons: one participating in the regional IGP, the other in the backbone IGP. The two would exchange routing information via EGP/BGP on a local loopback interface, achieving routing isolation without requiring separate hardware.
sections.eli5: The new, faster backbone works the same way as before, but now one smart router can do the job that used to require two separate pieces of equipment.

sections.title: How It Works in Practice
sections.content:
The proposed implementation would run two instances of routing daemons on a single routing engine. For NSFNET, one daemon would participate in the regional network's IGP, the other in the NSFNET backbone IGP. The two instances communicate with each other via EGP/BGP using the system's loopback interface (lo0 on UNIX).

The RFC emphasizes maintaining strong firewalls between the two IGP domains. IGP information must be tagged with exterior domain information at the boundary, and each side (NSFNET and the regional network) retains control over its own routing information. The Ethernet connection to the backbone serves as the administrative demarcation point between the two networks.
sections.eli5: Both routing languages run on the same machine. They talk to each other through an internal channel, like two people in the same room speaking different languages but understanding each other.

sections.title: Looking Ahead
sections.content:
The RFC suggests that future evolution could further simplify the interface. As NSFNET technology advances, the demarcation between backbone and client networks might move closer to the backbone's core. The E-NSS (exterior nodes) could eventually participate fully in the client network's IGP while the C-NSS (core nodes) handle only backbone routing.

For this to work, both the backbone provider and the client must be able to manage the physical link between them collaboratively. The RFC notes that evolution of Point-to-Point Protocol and enhanced network management capabilities will help. The goal is to make the demarcation point as easy to manage as a local Ethernet interface, simplifying deployment for client sites.
sections.eli5: In the future, the line between 'your network' and 'the backbone' could move, making it even simpler to connect. But that will require better management tools.
